newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Jan 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Jan 7.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- WOOLWICH WINDFALL '1,200 STG'

Almost 2.6 members of the Woolwich building society will receive windfall share pay-outs worth more than 1,200 stg when the group converts to a bank and floats in July. The figures are based on estimates from Schroders and BZW, adviser and broker, respectively, to Woolwich. The estimate suggests that the free shares bonanza this year from converting building societies could top 20 billion stg, 20 percent higher than expectations.
-- BLUE CIRCLE OFFERS JOB SECURITY LINK TO PAY DEAL

Unions have hailed as 'groundbreaking' a deal that offers employees of the cement group Blue Circle job security in return for annual pay increases of inflation plus a quarter percentage point over the next three years. Blue Circle already has a similar agreement with its 124 distribution drivers, which includes a promise of no more contracting out of haulage. The settlement, which is expected to be finalised this week, has also been welcomed by Labour shadow employment spokesman Peter Hain as 'agenda setting'.
-- BRUSSELS FIRM ON PROTEST OVER CUBA LAW

The European Commission is to continue pursuing its case against US anti-Cuba legislation at the World Trade Organisation despite concessions by Washington on the issue. The legislation, under the Helms-Burton act, gives Americans the right to sue foreigners who profited from property seized from Americans by the Cuban government. President Bill Clinton has twice suspended parts of the law in an effort to appease the EU, which is seeking a ruling from the WTO.
-- MILLENNIUM EXHIBITION FACES CRUNCH MEETING

The Millennium Commission is due to meet the Labour party next week in what could be a crunch meeting for the future of the proposed millennium exhibition at Greenwich, east London. The Commission is expected to present details of a revised business plan for the project after Labour demanded cuts in the budget before it could pledge to support the public funding of the project should the party win the forthcoming general election.
-- N-AGENCY MAY FACE PLUTONIUM LAWSUIT

The Health and Safety Executive has said that the Atomic Energy Authority, the state-owned body that operates the Dounreay nuclear reprocessing plant, could face prosecution over two incidents in which employees at the plant received overdoses of plutonium. An internal investigation into the incidents is being conducted by the AEA under HSE supervision, and the HSE will decide whether to prosecute following completion of the inquiry.
-- WELSH ACTIVISTS TO LOBBY ABBEY

Welsh language activists are planning to lobby the Abbey National bank over its approach to providing services in Welsh. The language and civil rights group Cefn surveyed all banks with branches in Wales over their policies, but chose to target the Abbey because of the coolness of its response. Cefn had also received complaints about monolingual signs inside and outside Abbey branches, and letters and statements written solely in English.
-- ORANGE AND ONE-2-ONE UP PACE

Figures out from Orange and One 2 One, the UK's youngest mobile phone operators, reveal that they took an unexpectedly large share of the market from rivals Vodafone and Cellnet last year. Orange reported a net gain of 125,000 subscribers in the fourth quarter of 1996 to 785,000. One 2 One gained a net 85,000 subscribers in the final quarter of the year, compared to an increase of 35,000 for the same period in 1995.
-- GA AIMS TO DOUBLE NEW PREMIUM INCOME

Insurer General Accident is aiming to double new premium income from sales of life assurance, pensions and investment products in the next three years. Details of the strategy, which may involve an acquisition to help reach the targets, are being finalised in a business plan. New premium income for GA in 1996 is believed to have topped 1 billion stg, and, according to assistant general manager Peter Hales, GA Life is planning growth of 20 percent to 25 percent this year.
-- RAYTHEON IN $2.95 BILLION OFFER FOR TEXAS INSTRUMENTS' ARM

US defence giant Raytheon has made an agreed $2.95bn (1.74 billion stg) offer for the military operations of Texas Instruments. The move takes the shake-out at the top of the US defence industry into its closing stages, with attention now centred on the expected bidding for the defence business of Hughes Electronics. Raytheon and Northrop Grumman are expected to battle for Hughes, the last 'available' large-scale defence contractor in the US industry, and the price for Hughes could well be pushed beyond the opening valuation of $9 billion.
-- COLD SNAP FAILS TO IGNITE GAS DEMAND

Officials at British Gas have said that it is too early to assess the impact of the recent very cold UK weather on the company's financial fortunes, but that demand over the period has been running at similar levels to the same time last year. On February 20, 1996, British Gas TransCo reported a record demand of 388m cubic meters, but the holiday shutdown by many industries this year prevented that record being broken.
